title: Capstone: Design Your Own Robot
description: Module 1 asked you to imagine a robot before you knew any electronics. Twelve modules later, design it again — this time knowing exactly how every part of it would actually work.

content.value: Go back and look at what you wrote in Module 1's Robot Concept Card if you still have it. That was an honest guess, made before you knew what a motor driver was for or why a caster ball beats a third wheel. This one doesn't have to guess.

Pick a real chore or problem, and design a robot for it — free-form, your own idea, no fixed right answer. The only requirement is that sense, think and act genuinely fit together, using real parts and real logic this course actually taught you.

content.title: 🎓 Capstone Robot
content.prompt: Name it, describe the problem, and fill in a real sense/think/act loop using parts and ideas from this whole course.

example.name: GardenGuard
example.job: checks whether the school garden's soil is dry and needs watering, without a human having to check by hand every day
example.sense: a soil-moisture sensor (wired the same way as any resistive sensor in Module 3) plus an ultrasonic sensor to avoid the flower beds while moving between rows
example.think: a while True: loop comparing the moisture reading to a threshold, deciding whether to trigger the pump
example.act: a relay switching a small water pump, and an RGB LED showing green (fine) or red (needs water) at a glance

fields.label: What real problem does it solve?
fields.placeholder: e.g. checks the garden's soil moisture

fields.label: SENSE: which real sensors, and why those?
fields.placeholder: e.g. a soil-moisture sensor and an ultrasonic sensor

fields.label: THINK: what's the actual decision logic?
fields.placeholder: e.g. while True: if moisture < threshold: ...

fields.label: ACT: what does it physically do?
fields.placeholder: e.g. switches a pump, lights an LED

content.value: Every field in that card traces back to something specific: SENSE to Modules 7-8, THINK to Modules 9-10, ACT to Modules 4-6, and the whole idea of the loop itself back to Module 1's very first lesson. If you can fill this card in confidently, you've genuinely completed this course — not just clicked through it.

There's no simulator run for this one, on purpose. Some of the best robot ideas — a robot for a genuinely unusual problem, using parts this course never built a widget for — can't be tested in twelve modules' worth of prebuilt worlds. The design itself is the achievement.

Key takeaway: a real robot design is nothing more than a sense/think/act loop, made of specific, real parts and real logic — the exact same three words this course opened with, now something you can fill in with genuine expertise.

quiz.question: Why does this final lesson deliberately echo Module 1's Robot Concept Card?
options: It's just recycled content with nothing new
It's the same exercise, but now answerable with real knowledge instead of a guess — proof of how far the course has taken you
Module 1's card was a mistake that needed correcting
quiz.explain: The structure repeats on purpose — filling it in with genuine, specific answers is the whole point of ending the course this way.

quiz.question: What's the actual requirement for the capstone design, beyond picking any idea?
options: It must use every single component from all twelve modules
Sense, think and act must genuinely fit together, using real parts and logic this course actually taught
It must be gradeable by an automated simulator
quiz.explain: There's no single right answer — the bar is coherence: a real loop, built from real ideas, not an exhaustive checklist.
